summary: The mechanism is BUILT AND COMPLETE, and it is PARKED ONE DIRECTORY FROM HOME, because this ticket cannot be satisfied by the seat it was dispatched to. The ticket's gate is `node scripts/loop-brief.selftest.mjs`; loop-work.yml's containment gate allows only ^(\.github/loop/(outbox|work)/|plant/), and a diff outside that is not rejected but DESTROYED — `git checkout -- . && git clean -fd`, which would have taken this outbox with it and left no trace that the turn ever happened. So writing to scripts/ was the one move guaranteed to produce nothing. I wrote the module and its gate to plant/tools/loop-brief.mjs and plant/tools/loop-brief.selftest.mjs instead; the module imports nothing and touches no filesystem, and the selftest imports './loop-brief.mjs', so finishing this ticket is TWO `git mv` and no edits. WHAT THE MECHANISM DOES: selection by lexical overlap, no model call. Ticket tokens are weighted by the field they came from (title 3, tags/gate 2, body 1, highest field wins rather than the sum); a finding scores the sum of ticket-term weights, doubled for a term in its title; findings sort by score then recency then id, and the top N=24 scoring at least MIN_SCORE=1 survive. MIN_SCORE is what makes this selection rather than truncation — a zero-overlap finding is dropped even when there is room under the cap. Every dead-end survives unconditionally, and every operator answer, and the file states the asymmetry rather than leaving it to be tuned away later. Bodies are clipped (findings 1600 chars, dead-ends 3200) with a note pointing at beads.jsonl, and the composed section ends with a footer stating how many findings were dropped, so the bound is never silent. THE GATE, and this is the part I want read: each of the ticket's three requirements is paired with a CONTROL, because an assertion that cannot fail is indistinguishable from one that passes. (a) the budget assertion is preceded by asserting that the CURRENT unselected behaviour blows the same 131072-byte budget by ~12x on the same fixture — without that, the budget check passes for a composer returning the empty string. (b) discrimination is demonstrated with 2 candidates against a cap of 24, so truncation cannot explain the outcome, and the unrelated finding's score is asserted to be EXACTLY 0 against a vocabulary I checked word by word against the ticket's full term list; §5 then repeats it under real pressure, keeping the OLDEST finding in a 502-finding ledger because it scores highest and dropping the NEWEST despite it clearing the threshold, which isolates score from recency in both directions. (c) every dead-end in the fixture is asserted to score EXACTLY 0 BEFORE asserting they all survive — otherwise 'the dead-ends survived' might only mean they were relevant and the exemption would never be exercised — and they survive again at maxFindings 0 with minScore 1e9. HONESTLY: I could not run any of it. No Bash. Every fixture is pure ASCII so byte length equals character length, and I hand-computed the composed size at roughly 85KB against the 131072 budget and the unselected control at roughly 1.66MB; every 'these two texts share no token' claim was checked against a hand-derived list of the ticket's terms that is written into the file so a reader can check my work rather than trust it. I deliberately did NOT put the selftest in plant/test/, where it would have been executed by this very run's whole-suite check: that glob also gates every future creates-gate turn and every deploy-plant publish, so an unrun, self-written test about loop infrastructure sitting in the game's suite could halt the fleet on three consecutive failures with nobody watching. Verification I could have had, traded for a blast radius I could not bound.

learned.title: The loop dispatched a ticket its own containment gate makes IMPOSSIBLE — and the destructive branch would have erased the evidence
learned.body:
lp-14c7f5 names `scripts/loop-brief.selftest.mjs` as the gate it creates. loop-work.yml's containment gate is a hardcoded regex, ^(\.github/loop/(outbox|work)/|plant/), and scripts/ is not in it. So the ticket is unsatisfiable by the seat it was dispatched to, and no amount of skill inside the turn changes that.

WHAT MAKES IT A DEAD-END RATHER THAN A BUG REPORT is the failure shape. The gate does not reject the offending file, it runs `git checkout -- . && git clean -fd` over the whole tree. `clean -fd` removes untracked files, and the outbox is an untracked file. So an agent that does the obvious, correct-looking thing — write the deliverable where the ticket says — loses the deliverable AND the outbox AND every finding it wrote, and the run reports gate=failed with no record of what was attempted. The next turn on the bead has no way to learn any of this and does the same thing.

SECOND-ORDER, AND WORSE, and it is why this bead may not exist to be read: loop-work applies the outbox to the ledger only `if outbox.valid && ticketgate != failed`. This ticket's gate is a command naming a file no seat can create, so ticketgate is failed WHATEVER the turn does. A blocked turn's learnings therefore never reach the ledger — the outbox JSON is committed to the branch (the staging step derives from config.writes, which covers .github/loop/) but nothing folds it into memory. A turn can be maximally honest about why it is blocked and the loop still forgets. If you are reading this at all, someone applied it by hand.

THIS IS THE SIXTH INSTANCE OF ONE PATTERN. The ledger already records five: the brief taught creates-gate and the outbox schema had no field; the reviewer could not wake the tick on a zero-promote; the worker's propose schema omitted class/gate; the planner could not wake the tick at all; every seat's push loop could not survive a conflict in a generated file. Each time a component was right and the CHANNEL between it and the next stage could not carry the result. This one is the same shape aimed at the WORK ITSELF rather than at a message: the ticket factory can express a requirement the executor is structurally forbidden to satisfy, and nothing between them compares the two.

THE CHEAP CHECK, and it belongs at dispatch, not here: loop-tick already knows the bead and can read config.json. Before issuing a work order, assert that every path a bead's `gate` names falls inside the containment regex. A bead whose gate lives outside the fleet's write scope is not dispatchable — fail closed, exactly as the class taxonomy does for an untagged bead. That is a few lines in the reactor and it would have converted a wasted turn into a correct 'nothing dispatchable, staff a human'.

AND THE DEEPER ONE: the containment regex and config.writes are TWO LISTS OF THE SAME THING, already drifted (writes has loop/**, containment does not). This repo has already paid for exactly this — loop-work's staging step used to be a hardcoded list that did not include plant/ and silently discarded the first live turn's entire output. The comment above that step now says the write set and the stage set must come from one source or they drift invisibly. The containment set is the third copy and it was not brought along.

learned.title: Parked the deliverable in plant/tools/ rather than plant/test/ — verification traded for a blast radius I could not bound
learned.body:
Both are inside containment, so both survive. The difference is that everything matching plant/test/*.selftest.mjs is executed by loop-work's whole-suite check on EVERY creates-gate turn, and by deploy-plant before it publishes. Putting the selftest there would have had it RUN in this very workflow run, and given I have no Bash that execution is the only real verification available to me — a genuinely large prize, and the ledger has roughly twenty findings complaining about exactly its absence.

I chose against it. The suite is plant's, and this file is loop infrastructure with nothing to do with the game. If my unrun, self-written test is wrong, it does not fail alone: it fails the gate of every future creates-gate turn and blocks every plant deploy, and stop.repeatedGateFailures is 3 — so a bug in a file about brief composition could halt the fleet, unattended, for a reason no later turn would connect to this one. The vision states plainly there is no human in the loop this run.

So: a bounded loss (my work is unverified, which is the loop's normal condition) against an unbounded one (the loop stops and nobody is there). I took the bounded loss.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a human, or any turn with Bash, running `node plant/tools/loop-brief.selftest.mjs` once. If it passes, moving it to scripts/ (its home) makes the question moot, because scripts/ selftests are not in plant's glob either. The trade only exists while the file is parked.

Second, smaller decision recorded here: the module imports NOTHING — not even scripts/lib/beads.mjs, whose bead shape it operates on — and touches no filesystem, purely so the pair is location-independent and the move home is two `git mv` with zero edits. That cost a little duplication of knowledge about the bead shape (kind, tags, title, body, created) and bought a mechanical, un-botchable move.

learned.title: N=24 and the clip lengths are the two numbers in this mechanism that no gate can justify — and only one of them is safe
learned.body:
The selection rule is testable end to end and the gate tests it. What the gate CANNOT say is whether 24 findings is the right number, or whether clipping a finding to 1600 characters keeps the part that mattered.

The cap is the safe one. It is a pure resource dial: too low and a turn is under-informed, too high and the brief creeps back toward the problem this ticket exists to fix, and either way the failure is gradual and reversible by editing one constant. Nothing depends on 24 being correct.

THE CLIP IS NOT SAFE, and it is worth separating from the cap because they look like the same kind of knob. The findings in this ledger are not uniformly dense: the load-bearing sentence of a long one is often at the END, after the narration of how it was discovered — 'the general shape, and it is the part that transfers', 'the transferable rule', 'the lesson, which is about the planner and not this turn'. A head-clip at 1600 characters takes the story and drops the moral, which is the precise inversion of what you would want. I chose head-clipping anyway because it is the only rule that needs no model call and cannot be wrong in a way that hides itself, and because the clip note points at beads.jsonl so nothing is actually lost to an agent willing to Read it.

The cheap improvement, if anyone wants it and it needs no model either: clip the MIDDLE, keeping the first ~900 and last ~700 characters with the elision marked between them. That preserves both the claim and the moral for the shape these findings actually have. I did not do it here because it is a second behaviour to test and this ticket's gate is already carrying three requirements, and because a middle-clip is a guess about document structure that I have evidence for but have not measured.

propose.title: Derive loop-work's containment gate from config.writes — the third copy of one list, and it has already drifted
propose.body:
loop-work.yml's containment ALLOWED regex is hardcoded as ^(\.github/loop/(outbox|work)/|plant/). .github/loop/config.json's `writes` says loop/**, .github/loop/**, plant/**. These are two statements of the same fact and they already disagree. The staging step three hundred lines below derives from `writes` precisely because a hardcoded copy of it silently discarded the first live turn's entire output, and the comment there says the write set and the stage set must come from one source or they drift invisibly. The containment set is the third copy and was not brought along.

WHY IT IS WORTH DOING BEYOND TIDINESS: it makes the fleet's write scope a single reviewable line in a JSON file rather than a regex buried in a workflow, which is the precondition for ever answering 'may the loop edit its own machinery' as a deliberate decision instead of by accident. Today the answer is 'no, in one place, and yes, in another'.

SCOPE, and this is the honest part: whoever takes this must decide whether widening containment to match `writes` (which adds loop/**) is intended, or whether `writes` should narrow to match containment. I believe the first — loop/ is the monitoring surface and its data file is generated by the same commit anyway — but that is a judgement about blast radius and it is the reviewer's, not mine.

THE GATE IT CREATES: scripts/loop-containment.selftest.mjs, asserting that the regex built from a given `writes` list (a) matches every path in that list's directories, (b) rejects foam/, scripts/, .github/workflows/ and docs/ when they are absent from it, (c) is anchored, so that a path merely CONTAINING an allowed prefix is refused, and (d) matches the regex literal currently in loop-work.yml when fed the current config, so the change is provably a refactor before it is a widening.

PRECONDITION, STATED PLAINLY: this touches .github/workflows/ and scripts/, both OUTSIDE the containment gate it is about. No agent seat can execute it — the change is its own blocker. It needs an operator, or it needs to be sequenced after the write scope is widened. Do not dispatch it to the fleet expecting it to land; it will produce exactly the outcome lp-14c7f5 produced.

propose.title: Refuse to dispatch a bead whose gate names a file outside the fleet's write scope
propose.body:
lp-14c7f5 was dispatched with the gate `node scripts/loop-brief.selftest.mjs`. No agent seat can create a file in scripts/. The turn was therefore unsatisfiable before it started, and it cost a full turn of model budget to discover that from the inside.

loop-tick already has everything needed to catch it: it reads the bead (it filters on class and tags) and it reads config.json (it reads the budget block). The check is: for each command in the bead's `gate`, take every token ending in a source extension — the same conservative token rule `beads promote` already uses for its existence check — and assert the path falls inside the containment scope. If it does not, the bead is NOT DISPATCHABLE. Fail closed, exactly as an untagged bead is treated as not-class-A: the cost of being wrong is a bead that sits still, which is visible and cheap, and the cost of the current behaviour is a wasted turn that reports gate=failed for a reason nobody can act on.

WHY THE REACTOR AND NOT PROMOTION: promotion is a good place for it too and already has a filesystem. But promotion happened for this bead when the operator wrote it, and the scope can change afterwards — a path can leave the write set. The reactor is the last point before spend, and the ledger's own hardest-won budget lesson is that the meter belongs at the point of spend rather than at a downstream component that may never run. Same argument, same place.

SECOND HALF, AND IT IS THE HALF THAT PAYS: a blocked turn's outbox is currently DISCARDED. loop-work applies the outbox only if ticketgate != failed, and a bead whose gate names an unreachable file fails its gate whatever the turn does — so a turn that correctly diagnoses its own impossibility has its diagnosis dropped on the floor, and the next turn rediscovers it. Applying the `learned` array on a gate failure, while still refusing to mark the bead done, would close that. A failed turn's findings are the most valuable thing it produces; they are exactly the thing this system is built to keep.

THE GATE — and note it is NOT a new one: scripts/loop-tick.selftest.mjs already exists and passes, so this is class-a proper (certified against an existing gate) with assertions added to it rather than creates-gate work — assert that a fixture bead gated on scripts/x.mjs is not dispatchable under a config whose writes are plant/**, that the same bead IS dispatchable once scripts/** is added, that a gate naming no path at all (e.g. `test -f plant/index.html`) is unaffected, and that a grep pattern containing a slash is not mistaken for a path.

PRECONDITION: touches scripts/ and is therefore outside the fleet's write scope today, same as its sibling above. Operator work until that changes.

asks.title: May the loop write its own machinery? This turn is the first time the answer mattered, and it is a risk judgement no gate can make
asks.body: Every agent seat is confined to plant/ plus its outbox. That boundary is what keeps a turn off the public web and out of the workflows that spend money, and it is stated as a security property rather than a convenience. It is also, as of this turn, the thing that makes a whole class of ticket unsatisfiable: lp-14c7f5 asks for a file in scripts/, the reactor happily dispatched it, and no possible turn could have delivered it. The three proposals this turn and the last few have produced about the loop's own plumbing are all in the same position. This is not decidable from inside a turn because it is not a question about correctness — the mechanism is easy to build either way — it is a question about how much of its own machinery you are willing to let an unattended fleet edit while you are asleep, and only you can price that.
asks.do: Open .github/workflows/loop-work.yml at the containment gate (the ALLOWED regex, around line 314) and .github/loop/config.json's `writes` array, and read them side by side. Then run `node plant/tools/loop-brief.selftest.mjs` — the deliverable this turn parked — and decide whether you would have been comfortable with an unattended turn writing that file into scripts/ and a later one wiring it into the brief every seat reads.
asks.watch: Specifically whether the loop editing the code that composes its own prompt feels different in kind from the loop editing plant/. I think it does and I could not tell you where the line is: a turn that changes what turns are told is the one edit whose mistakes are invisible to every gate downstream of it, because everything downstream reads the output of the thing that broke.
asks.soThat: If the answer is NO, then the two proposals above are permanently operator work and should be tagged human-only rather than sitting in the queue looking dispatchable — and the reactor's fix from proposal 2 becomes the important one, because it stops the loop wasting turns on tickets it cannot reach. If the answer is YES BUT NARROWLY — say, scripts/loop-*.mjs and nothing else — then the containment regex should come from config.writes (proposal 1) and you add that one glob, and this ticket finishes itself on the next dispatch. If the answer is YES BROADLY, the write scope and the staging list and the containment regex should collapse into one list today, before a fourth copy of it appears.
